cover.body_html:
8月5日，硅谷地震。

Jeff Dean，Google第30号员工、在公司待了整整27年的传奇工程师、MapReduce和TensorFlow的缔造者、Google AI帝国的总设计师，正式宣布离职。他不是一个人走的——和他一起离开的还有三位顶级科学家：Sanjay Ghemawat（Google Senior Fellow，Jeff Dean二十多年的黄金搭档）、Quoc Le（Google Brain创始成员，Seq2Seq和AutoML的发明者）、Oriol Vinyals（DeepMind高级研究科学家，AlphaStar和Gemini多模态核心负责人）。

四个人加起来，在Google的工作年限超过80年。他们参与或主导了Google过去二十年几乎所有最重要的基础设施和AI项目：从BigTable、Spanner到TensorFlow，从Transformer之前的分布式训练框架到Gemini多模态，从AlphaGo到AlphaFold。你可以说，这四个人就是Google AI的半壁江山。

他们的新公司叫Discovery Loop，注册为公益公司（Public Benefit Corporation），专注方向是AI for Science——用AI自动化科学发现。Jeff Dean亲自担任CEO。投资方阵容豪华到离谱：Radical Ventures和Khosla Ventures联合领投，Kleiner Perkins、Lightspeed、Doerr Capital跟投，甚至连老东家Alphabet都参投了。

消息公布当天，Alphabet股价盘中下跌约4-5%，市值蒸发数百亿美元。而就在同一时间，Google还宣布了另一则人事变动：Demis Hassabis卸任Google DeepMind CEO，转任Google DeepMind董事长兼Alphabet首席科学家，继续领导Isomorphic Labs。DeepMind CEO一职由Koray Kavukcuoglu接任。

一天之内，Google AI的两大支柱——Google Research和DeepMind——同时换帅。一个时代结束了。

Jeff和Sanjay：Google工程文化的活化石

要理解Jeff Dean离职的分量，你得先理解Jeff和Sanjay这对组合在Google意味着什么。

1999年，Jeff Dean加入Google，是公司第30号员工。那时候Google还在一个车库里办公，拉里·佩奇和谢尔盖·布林还在斯坦福读博没毕业。几年后Sanjay Ghemawat加入，两人开始了长达二十多年的传奇搭档。在Google内部，"Jeff和Sanjay"是一个专有名词——他们共用一个办公室（直到远程办公时代），代码提交记录经常分不清是谁写的，甚至有人开玩笑说他们是一个人用两个账号。

这对搭档在2000年代初做的一系列工作，定义了整个互联网时代的基础设施：MapReduce让大规模分布式数据处理变得简单，BigTable开创了NoSQL数据库的先河，Spanner实现了全球一致性分布式数据库，TensorFlow把深度学习从学术圈带到了工业界。这些项目每一个单拎出来，都足以让一个工程师名垂青史。而Jeff和Sanjay两个人，一起做了四五个。

在Google工程师文化里，Jeff Dean是神一样的存在。内部流传着无数关于他的段子："Jeff Dean的代码编译时不会警告，因为编译器不敢警告他""Jeff Dean曾经在O(1)时间内解决了NP完全问题""有一次Jeff Dean的键盘坏了，他用二进制0和1直接写了一个操作系统"。这些段子当然是夸张的，但背后是整个公司对他技术能力的绝对崇拜。

Quoc Le是另一个传奇。2011年他从斯坦福加入Google，是Google Brain创始成员之一。他和Ilya Sutskever、Alex Krizhevsky等人一起师从Andrew Ng，是深度学习黄金一代的代表人物。Seq2Seq模型是他做的，这直接催生了神经机器翻译；AutoML是他推动的，开启了用AI设计AI的方向；他在Google内部带过的团队和项目，几乎覆盖了Google AI的半壁江山。

Oriol Vinyals来自DeepMind体系。他是AlphaStar（《星际争霸》AI）的第一作者，是Gemini多模态能力的核心负责人之一，也是序列建模和强化学习领域的顶级科学家。他的离开意味着DeepMind和Google Research之间的人才流动通道，这次变成了向外的单向出口。

四个人同时离开，这在Google历史上是前所未有的。哪怕是2023年Ilya Sutskever在OpenAI政变风波后离职创办Safe Superintelligence，也只带走了几个人。Jeff Dean这次是直接把Google AI最核心的一个小圈子整体端走了。

为什么走？大公司的AI创新困境

表面上看，官方说法很体面：Jeff Dean想专注于AI for Science这个他个人 passion 所在的方向，大公司的组织结构不适合做这种高风险长周期的探索；Sundar Pichai发公开信感谢他27年的贡献，Alphabet甚至参与投资，一副"好聚好散"的画面。

"当你在Google内部做一个新项目，需要12个VP审批、6个季度对齐OKR、3轮法务审查的时候，你就知道为什么顶级研究者要出去创业了。"—— 一位前Google AI研究员

但了解Google内部情况的人都知道，这不是一次和平分手那么简单。过去两年，Google AI一直处于一种尴尬的防守姿态：OpenAI的ChatGPT横空出世打了Google一个措手不及，Gemini发布后口碑起起伏伏，搜索产品被AI重构的过程中内部矛盾重重，越来越多的顶级研究者选择离开。

大公司AI创新的结构性困境，在Google身上体现得淋漓尽致。

第一，组织惯性和决策缓慢。在Google做一个新项目，从立项到资源到位，往往需要半年甚至更长时间。你需要对齐无数个VP的OKR，需要和其他部门抢资源，需要应对法务、隐私、安全等各种部门的审查。而创业公司可以在一周内决定方向、两周内开始动手、一个月内出第一个版本。对于Jeff Dean这种级别的人来说，时间比钱宝贵得多——他已经50多岁了，财务自由早就实现了，剩下的职业生涯想做真正有影响力的事，大公司的组织效率显然满足不了他。

第二，产品化压力挤压基础研究。Gemini发布后，Google Research和DeepMind的资源明显向产品端倾斜。搜索、广告、云、Workspace，每一个产品线都在喊着要AI能力，研究者们被拉去做各种产品集成和优化，能沉下心做长周期基础研究的空间越来越小。Jeff Dean一直想大力投入AI for Science，但在产品优先级永远高于研究的大公司环境里，这个方向始终得不到足够的资源和自主权。

第三，薪酬和激励机制的落后。OpenAI给顶级研究者开出的年薪包裹动辄数千万美元甚至上亿美元，Anthropic、xAI、各种AI创业公司都在用天价包裹挖人。Google的薪酬体系虽然在大厂里算顶级的，但和这些AI新贵相比还是差了一个量级。更重要的是，在大公司你能拿到的回报是线性的——你做出了TensorFlow这样改变世界的项目，拿到的奖金和股票也不过是包裹里的几个百分点增长；而在创业公司，你有可能拿到1%甚至10%的股权，项目成功了就是十亿甚至百亿美元级别的回报。

第四，DeepMind和Google Research的内耗。2014年收购DeepMind后，Google内部就一直存在Google Brain（后来的Google Research）和DeepMind两套体系的竞争与内耗。两边研究方向重叠、资源争夺、文化冲突，直到2023年才在Alphabet层面合并为Google DeepMind，但整合效果并不理想。Jeff Dean作为Google Research的负责人，和Demis Hassabis作为DeepMind的负责人，两人之间的权力平衡一直很微妙。这次两人同时"卸任"，一个出去创业，一个升任董事长+首席科学家，某种程度上也是这种内部博弈的最终结果。

Discovery Loop的赌注：AI for Science是下一个金矿吗？

Jeff Dean选择AI for Science作为创业方向，这个选择本身就很值得玩味。

过去两年，AI大模型的商业落地主要集中在内容生成、聊天机器人、编程助手、企业服务这些方向。但越来越多的人开始意识到，AI真正能产生指数级价值的领域可能是科学发现——药物研发、材料科学、气候建模、核聚变、基因组学。这些领域每一个突破都可能带来万亿美元级别的市场，而传统科学方法已经到了瓶颈期，AI是破局的唯一希望。

Isomorphic Labs（Demis Hassabis领导的DeepMind分拆公司）已经在AI药物研发上取得了不少进展；AlphaFold解决了蛋白质折叠问题，这本身就是AI for Science的里程碑；OpenAI也成立了专门的科学团队；各大制药公司都在疯狂布局AI药物研发。但目前还没有一家公司把"AI驱动科学发现全流程自动化"作为核心使命，Discovery Loop瞄准的就是这个空白。

Jeff Dean的优势在哪里？第一，他是系统级工程师出身，不是纯算法研究者——他懂得怎么构建大规模分布式系统，怎么把AI模型和真实的科学实验流程结合起来，而不仅仅是在benchmark上刷分数。第二，他在Google积累了二十年的基础设施经验，知道怎么搭建能支撑千名科学家、亿级实验的平台。第三，他的个人品牌和人脉能吸引到全世界最顶尖的科学家和工程师加入。

当然，这个方向的风险也极大。科学发现不像做聊天机器人，周期极长——一个新药研发平均需要10年以上，一个新材料从发现到产业化可能需要15-20年。Discovery Loop作为一家创业公司，能不能扛过这么长的周期，能不能在烧完融资前拿出真正有商业价值的成果，都是未知数。

但从投资方的阵容来看，资本已经在用脚投票了。Radical Ventures是AI领域最顶级的VC之一，投过DeepMind、OpenAI（早期）、Anthropic等几乎所有重要AI公司；Khosla Ventures是Vinod Khosla创办的，以押注高风险高回报的颠覆性技术著称；Alphabet的跟投更是耐人寻味——相当于Google自己也承认：这个方向在Google内部做不成，只能靠独立公司去做。

Hassabis交权：DeepMind的后创始人时代

和Jeff Dean离职同一天宣布的Demis Hassabis卸任消息，同样值得关注。

很多中文媒体把这件事解读为"Hassabis被架空""DeepMind创始人被赶走"，这是不准确的。官方公告里写得很清楚：Hassabis升任Google DeepMind董事长，同时担任Alphabet首席科学家，继续全职领导Isomorphic Labs。Koray Kavukcuoglu接任DeepMind CEO，他是DeepMind的创始成员之一，在DeepMind工作了超过15年，是内部培养起来的接班人。

这更像是一次正常的权力交接和职责调整。Hassabis今年已经50岁了，2010年创办DeepMind至今已经16年，AlphaGo、AlphaFold、AlphaStar这些标志性成果都是他领导下做出来的，但DeepMind被收购后整合进Google的这几年，他的精力更多放在了Alphabet层面的AI战略和Isomorphic Labs上，日常管理工作确实需要有人接手。

但这个时间点和Jeff Dean离职撞在一起，还是难免让人产生联想。一天之内，Google AI两大体系的一号人物同时离开日常管理岗位——一个彻底出走，一个退居二线——这标志着Google AI的"创始人时代"彻底结束了。接下来的Google DeepMind，将进入职业经理人主导的时代。

这对Google AI来说是好事还是坏事？短期来看肯定有阵痛。Jeff Dean和Hassabis这种级别的人物，他们的技术判断力、个人魅力和对人才的吸引力是不可替代的。但长期来看，任何大公司都要经历创始人交棒的过程，关键是接班人能不能延续原来的文化和创新能力。Koray是DeepMind老人，技术背景过硬，内部威望也够，但他能不能在大公司的产品压力下保住DeepMind的研究基因，这要打个问号。

人才地震的连锁反应：大模型时代的人才流动新常态

Jeff Dean的离开不是孤立事件，它是过去两年AI行业人才大流动的一个缩影，也是一个新的高潮。

2023年以来，我们已经见证了太多顶级AI人才的出走：Ilya Sutskever离开OpenAI创办SSI；Dario Amodei虽然还在Anthropic但已经在考虑接班人问题；一大批OpenAI、Google、Meta的研究员出去创办自己的AI公司；甚至连高校里的教授都坐不住了，纷纷停薪留职下海。AI行业正在重演半导体行业、互联网行业曾经发生过的故事：当一个新技术浪潮到来时，最顶尖的人才会从大公司流向创业公司，因为那里有更大的自由度、更高的回报、更快的迭代速度。

对于大公司来说，这是一个无解的难题。你可以给员工发更高的工资、更多的股票，但你给不了他们时间自主权、决策速度和改变世界的机会感。当一个顶级人才已经财务自由之后，钱就不再是最重要的激励因素了——他们想要的是：我想做的项目能不能立刻开始？我做的决定能不能不被12个VP否决？我做成了一件事能不能拿到足够的credit和回报？这些恰恰是大公司最难提供的东西。

当然，大公司不会因此衰落。Google有最雄厚的算力资源、最多的数据、最成熟的商业化渠道，哪怕走了几个顶级人才，它依然是AI竞赛的第一梯队玩家。但人才流失的长期影响是潜移默化的：当最有创造力、最敢想敢干的那批人都走了，大公司的创新能力会慢慢钝化，最终变成一个守成的、优化效率的机构，而不是开拓新边疆的先锋。

对创业者和投资人来说，Jeff Dean的出走是一个强烈的信号：AI for Science这个赛道要热起来了。未来一两年，我们会看到越来越多的AI创业公司瞄准科学发现方向，资本会疯狂涌入，这个领域会重复过去两年大模型和AI编程赛道的剧本。

对于Google来说，这是一个时代的结束。那个在车库里创业、工程师文化至上、敢于做十年磨一剑项目的Google，正在慢慢变成一个成熟的、庞大的、商业驱动的科技巨头。这是所有伟大公司成长的必经之路，但还是难免让人感慨。

Jeff Dean在Google的27年，几乎就是一部Google工程和AI的发展史。他走的时候，没有愤怒，没有撕逼，甚至老东家还给他的新公司投了钱。但所有人都知道：有些东西已经永远改变了。

明天见。
cover.body_html_en:
August 5. Silicon Valley had an earthquake.

Jeff Dean — Google employee #30, the legendary engineer who spent 27 years at the company, architect of MapReduce and TensorFlow, the chief designer of Google's AI empire — officially announced his departure. And he didn't leave alone. Walking out with him were three top scientists: Sanjay Ghemawat (Google Senior Fellow, Jeff Dean's legendary partner of over two decades), Quoc Le (Google Brain founding member, inventor of Seq2Seq and AutoML), and Oriol Vinyals (DeepMind senior research scientist, lead on AlphaStar and Gemini multimodal).

Together, these four people represent over 80 years of combined tenure at Google. They participated in or led virtually every major infrastructure and AI project at Google over the past two decades: from BigTable and Spanner to TensorFlow, from pre-Transformer distributed training frameworks to Gemini multimodal, from AlphaGo to AlphaFold. You could say these four people are half of Google's AI brain trust.

Their new company is called Discovery Loop, incorporated as a Public Benefit Corporation, focused on AI for Science — using AI to automate scientific discovery. Jeff Dean himself will serve as CEO. The investor lineup is absurdly stacked: Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures co-leading, with Kleiner Perkins, Lightspeed, Doerr Capital participating, and even Alphabet, their former employer, chipping in.

On the day of the announcement, Alphabet's stock dropped roughly 4–5% intraday, wiping out tens of billions in market cap. And at the same time, Google announced another personnel change: Demis Hassabis is stepping down as CEO of Google DeepMind, becoming chairman of Google DeepMind and Alphabet Chief Scientist while continuing to lead Isomorphic Labs. Koray Kavukcuoglu takes over as DeepMind CEO.

In a single day, the two pillars of Google AI — Google Research and DeepMind — changed leadership simultaneously. An era has ended.

Jeff and Sanjay: Living Fossils of Google's Engineering Culture

To understand the weight of Jeff Dean's departure, you first have to understand what Jeff and Sanjay meant at Google.

Jeff Dean joined Google in 1999 as employee #30. Back then Google was operating out of a garage; Larry Page and Sergey Brin were still PhD students at Stanford and hadn't even graduated yet. A few years later Sanjay Ghemawat joined, and the pair began a legendary partnership that spanned over two decades. Inside Google, "Jeff and Sanjay" is a proper noun — they shared an office (until the remote work era), code commits were often indistinguishable between the two, and there were jokes that they were one person using two accounts.

A series of projects this pair built in the early 2000s defined the infrastructure of the entire internet era: MapReduce made large-scale distributed data processing simple; BigTable pioneered the NoSQL database movement; Spanner achieved globally consistent distributed databases; TensorFlow brought deep learning from academia to industry. Any one of these projects alone would be enough to cement an engineer's place in history. Jeff and Sanjay, together, built four or five.

In Google's engineering culture, Jeff Dean is a deity. Countless internal jokes circulate about him: "Jeff Dean's code doesn't generate warnings because compilers don't dare warn him"; "Jeff Dean once solved an NP-complete problem in O(1) time"; "When Jeff Dean's keyboard broke once, he wrote an operating system directly in binary 0s and 1s." These jokes are obviously exaggerated, but beneath them is the entire company's absolute reverence for his technical ability.

Quoc Le is another legend. He joined Google from Stanford in 2011 as one of the founding members of Google Brain. Alongside Ilya Sutskever, Alex Krizhevsky, and others, he studied under Andrew Ng and is a representative figure of deep learning's golden generation. Seq2Seq was his work, which directly spawned neural machine translation; he drove AutoML, opening the direction of AI designing AI; the teams and projects he's led inside Google cover virtually half of Google AI.

Oriol Vinyals comes from the DeepMind side. He was first author on AlphaStar (the StarCraft AI), one of the core leads on Gemini's multimodal capabilities, and a top scientist in sequence modeling and reinforcement learning. His departure means the talent pipeline between DeepMind and Google Research has become a one-way exit outward.

Four people leaving simultaneously is unprecedented in Google's history. Even when Ilya Sutskever left OpenAI after the 2023 boardroom coup to found Safe Superintelligence, he only took a handful of people. Jeff Dean essentially took Google AI's most core inner circle and walked it out the door.

Why Leave? Big Tech's AI Innovation Dilemma

On the surface, the official narrative is very dignified: Jeff Dean wants to focus on AI for Science, his personal passion, and large-company organizational structures aren't suited to this kind of high-risk, long-cycle exploration; Sundar Pichai published an open letter thanking him for 27 years of contributions, Alphabet even participated in the investment — a picture of "conscious uncoupling."

"When launching a new project inside Google requires 12 VP approvals, six quarters of OKR alignment, and three rounds of legal review, you understand why top researchers go start companies."— A former Google AI researcher

But anyone familiar with Google's internal situation knows this isn't just an amicable parting. Over the past two years, Google AI has been in an awkward defensive posture: OpenAI's ChatGPT caught Google flat-footed, Gemini's reputation has been rocky post-launch, the AI restructuring of search has been rife with internal friction, and more and more top researchers are choosing to leave.

The structural dilemma of AI innovation at big companies is on full display at Google.

First, organizational inertia and slow decision-making. Getting a new project off the ground at Google, from approval to resource allocation, often takes six months or more. You need to align with countless VPs' OKRs, compete for resources with other departments, and navigate reviews from legal, privacy, security, and various other departments. A startup can decide on a direction in a week, start building in two weeks, and have a first version in a month. For someone at Jeff Dean's level, time is far more valuable than money — he's in his 50s, financially independent long ago, and for the rest of his career he wants to work on things that truly matter. Big-company organizational efficiency clearly can't satisfy that.

Second, productization pressure squeezes basic research. After Gemini launched, resources at Google Research and DeepMind clearly tilted toward product. Search, ads, cloud, Workspace — every product line is screaming for AI capabilities, and researchers are pulled into product integrations and optimizations, leaving less and less space to focus on long-cycle basic research. Jeff Dean has long wanted to invest heavily in AI for Science, but in a big-company environment where product priorities always trump research, this direction never got sufficient resources or autonomy.

Third, outdated compensation and incentive structures. OpenAI offers top researchers annual packages in the tens of millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars; Anthropic, xAI, and various AI startups are all poaching with eye-popping packages. Google's compensation is top-tier among big tech, but it's still an order of magnitude behind these AI upstarts. More importantly, returns at big companies are linear — you build a world-changing project like TensorFlow and your bonus and stock go up a few percentage points; at a startup, you could get 1% or even 10% equity, and success means billions or tens of billions in returns.

Fourth, internal friction between DeepMind and Google Research. Since acquiring DeepMind in 2014, Google has always had two competing systems — Google Brain (later Google Research) and DeepMind — with overlapping research directions, resource fights, and cultural clashes. They were only merged into Google DeepMind at the Alphabet level in 2023, and integration has been less than smooth. As head of Google Research, Jeff Dean and Demis Hassabis as head of DeepMind maintained a delicate balance of power. Both "stepping down" from day-to-day management on the same day — one leaving entirely, the other moving to chairman + chief scientist — is to some extent the final outcome of this internal jockeying.

Discovery Loop's Bet: Is AI for Science the Next Gold Mine?

That Jeff Dean chose AI for Science as his startup direction is itself worth examining.

Over the past two years, commercial AI deployment has focused mainly on content generation, chatbots, coding assistants, and enterprise services. But more and more people are realizing that the area where AI can truly deliver exponential value may be scientific discovery — drug development, materials science, climate modeling, nuclear fusion, genomics. Every breakthrough in these fields could create trillion-dollar markets, and traditional scientific methods have hit bottlenecks; AI is the only hope for breaking through.

Isomorphic Labs (led by Demis Hassabis as a DeepMind spinout) has already made progress in AI drug discovery; AlphaFold solving protein folding is itself an AI for Science milestone; OpenAI has formed a dedicated science team; every major pharmaceutical company is furiously investing in AI drug R&D. But no company has yet made "full-process automation of AI-driven scientific discovery" its core mission, and Discovery Loop is targeting precisely this gap.

Where does Jeff Dean have an edge? First, he's a systems engineer by background, not a pure algorithm researcher — he knows how to build large-scale distributed systems, how to integrate AI models with real scientific experiment workflows, not just chase benchmark scores. Second, he has twenty years of infrastructure experience at Google and knows how to build platforms that can support a thousand scientists and a hundred million experiments. Third, his personal brand and network can attract the world's top scientists and engineers.

Of course, the risks in this direction are enormous. Scientific discovery isn't like building chatbots; cycles are extremely long — a new drug takes 10+ years on average; a new material from discovery to industrialization could take 15–20 years. Whether Discovery Loop as a startup can survive such long cycles and produce genuinely commercially valuable results before burning through funding is an open question.

But judging from the investor lineup, capital is already voting with its feet. Radical Ventures is one of the top VCs in AI, having backed DeepMind, OpenAI (early), Anthropic, and virtually every major AI company; Khosla Ventures, founded by Vinod Khosla, is known for betting on high-risk, high-reward disruptive technologies; Alphabet's participation is particularly telling — it's essentially Google admitting this direction can't be done inside Google; it can only be done by an independent company.

Hassabis Steps Back: DeepMind's Post-Founder Era

Demis Hassabis stepping down as DeepMind CEO, announced the same day as Jeff Dean's departure, is equally noteworthy.

Many Chinese media outlets framed this as "Hassabis being sidelined" or "the DeepMind founder being pushed out," which is inaccurate. The official announcement is clear: Hassabis is promoted to Chairman of Google DeepMind while serving as Alphabet Chief Scientist and continuing to lead Isomorphic Labs full-time. Koray Kavukcuoglu takes over as DeepMind CEO; he's one of DeepMind's founding members, has been at DeepMind for over 15 years, and is a successor groomed from within.

This looks more like a normal leadership transition and responsibility realignment. Hassabis is 50 this year; he founded DeepMind in 2010, 16 years ago. AlphaGo, AlphaFold, AlphaStar — all the landmark achievements happened under his leadership. But in the years since DeepMind was acquired and integrated into Google, his focus has shifted more toward Alphabet-level AI strategy and Isomorphic Labs, and day-to-day management genuinely needed someone to take over.

Still, the timing colliding with Jeff Dean's departure inevitably invites speculation. In a single day, the heads of both major Google AI systems left day-to-day management — one departing entirely, one moving to a chairman role — marking the definitive end of Google AI's "founder era." What comes next for Google DeepMind is an era led by professional managers.

Is this good or bad for Google AI? There will definitely be short-term growing pains. People at Jeff Dean and Hassabis's level have irreplaceable technical judgment, personal charisma, and ability to attract talent. But in the long run, every great company goes through founder succession. The question is whether successors can carry forward the original culture and innovative capacity. Koray is a DeepMind veteran with strong technical credentials and sufficient internal prestige, but whether he can preserve DeepMind's research DNA under big-company product pressure remains an open question.

The Talent Earthquake's Ripple Effects: The New Normal of Talent Flow in the LLM Era

Jeff Dean's departure isn't an isolated event; it's a microcosm — and a new climax — of the massive AI talent migration over the past two years.

Since 2023, we've already seen too many top AI talents depart: Ilya Sutskever left OpenAI to found SSI; Dario Amodei is still at Anthropic but already considering succession; a flood of researchers from OpenAI, Google, and Meta have left to found their own AI companies; even university professors can't sit still, taking leaves of absence to jump into the fray. The AI industry is repeating what happened in semiconductors and the internet before it: when a new technology wave arrives, the most talented people flow from big companies to startups, because that's where there's more autonomy, higher returns, and faster iteration.

For big companies, this is an unsolvable problem. You can pay employees higher salaries and more stock, but you can't give them autonomy over their time, decision speed, or the sense of opportunity to change the world. Once a top talent is financially independent, money is no longer the primary motivator — what they want is: Can the project I want to work on start immediately? Can the decisions I make not be vetoed by 12 VPs? When I build something, can I get sufficient credit and reward? These are precisely the things big companies struggle most to provide.

Of course, big companies won't decline because of this. Google has the most formidable compute resources, the most data, the most mature commercialization channels. Even losing a few top people, it remains a first-tier player in the AI race. But the long-term effects of brain drain are subtle: when the most creative, boldest people leave, big companies' innovative capacity gradually atrophies, eventually becoming institutions that maintain and optimize rather than pioneer new frontiers.

For founders and investors, Jeff Dean's exit is a strong signal: the AI for Science sector is about to heat up. Over the next year or two, we'll see more and more AI startups targeting scientific discovery, capital will flood in, and this field will repeat the script of the foundation model and AI coding sectors over the past two years.

For Google, this is the end of an era. The Google that started in a garage, that put engineering culture above all, that dared to do decade-in-the-making projects, is slowly becoming a mature, massive, commercially driven tech giant. This is the inevitable path of all great companies, but it's hard not to feel a sense of loss.

Jeff Dean's 27 years at Google are practically a history of Google engineering and AI. He left without anger, without public drama, and his old employer even invested in his new company. But everyone knows: something has changed forever.

See you tomorrow.

briefs.body_html:
AI编程Agent战场又杀进来一位重量级玩家。

8月5日，Meta正式发布首款AI编程Agent产品Muse Code，开启公测。这是Scale AI创始人Alexandr Wang今年初加入Meta担任超级智能实验室负责人后，交出的第一份重磅产品答卷。目标非常明确：做Claude Code和OpenAI Codex的低价替代方案。

扎克伯格在社交媒体上的表态很直接："Muse Code能帮你在大型代码库里完成真正的软件工程任务，不只是补全几行代码。"从目前放出的信息来看，这不是又一个Copilot式的代码补全工具，而是一个真正能自主完成重构、debug、新功能开发的全流程Agent。

持久后台Agent：核心差异化在哪？

Muse Code最大的技术亮点是持久后台Agent（persistent background agents）架构。

什么意思？现在市面上大多数AI编程工具（包括Claude Code和早期的Codex）的工作模式是：你发一个指令，它spawn一个新的Agent实例，完成任务后这个实例就销毁了。下次你再发指令，又是一个全新的Agent，不记得上次做了什么、你的代码库是什么结构、你的编码风格是什么样的。

Muse Code不一样。它的Agent是长期运行在后台的——它会持续学习你的代码库结构、记住你之前的修改偏好、理解整个项目的架构设计，甚至能主动发现代码里的问题并提出优化建议。跨session保持上下文，这是一个非常关键的架构差异。

打个比方：其他工具像是你每次都临时找一个外包程序员，干完活就走人，下次来的是另一个人；Muse Code像是你招了一个全职的资深工程师，他一直在你的团队里，越干越懂你的项目。对于大型代码库（百万行级别）来说，这种持续上下文积累带来的效率提升是巨大的——Agent不需要每次都花大量token重新索引和理解代码库。

第二个差异化是价格。Meta没有公布具体定价，但明确表示会"显著低于"Claude Code和Codex的价格。考虑到Meta一贯的开源和低价策略（Llama系列模型几乎是开源界的事实标准），Muse Code很可能会用价格战快速抢占市场份额。对于企业用户来说，AI编程工具的成本现在已经是一笔不小的开支——Uber四个月烧完全年AI编程预算的新闻还历历在目，一个更便宜的替代方案出现，吸引力是巨大的。

AI编程从Copilot时代进入Agent时代

Muse Code的入场，标志着AI编程正式从"Copilot时代"进入"Agent时代"。

2021-2024年是Copilot时代：AI的角色是"助手"，你写代码它补全，你需要时刻盯着、纠正着、引导着，本质上还是人在主导，AI做加速。2025年下半年开始，我们进入了Agent时代：AI的角色变成了"执行者"，你给一个高层级的任务描述，它自己拆解、自己规划、自己写代码、自己跑测试、自己debug，你只需要验收结果。

Claude Code是这个时代的第一个标杆产品，它证明了AI Agent确实能在真实生产环境里完成复杂的软件工程任务。OpenAI Codex紧随其后，凭借GPT系列模型的能力快速追赶。现在Muse Code杀进来，加上Cursor、Windsurf、Aider等一众创业公司产品，AI编程Agent赛道已经拥挤不堪。

但Meta的优势是别人比不了的。第一，它有Llama系列开源模型的生态——Muse Code底层可以用Llama 4，企业客户可以私有化部署，不用担心代码泄露给第三方。第二，Alexandr Wang的加入带来了Scale AI在数据标注和模型评估方面的深厚积累——AI编程Agent最核心的能力不是写代码，而是知道自己写的代码对不对，Scale的评估能力正好补上这块短板。第三，Meta自己就是全球最大的代码生产者之一——Facebook、Instagram、WhatsApp都是亿级用户的产品，Muse Code可以先在Meta内部几十亿行代码上打磨，成熟了再对外开放，这是纯创业公司没有的优势。

"2024年大家比谁的代码补全更准，2026年大家比谁的Agent更能独立扛下一个完整功能。"—— 一位AI编程工具创业者

当然，Muse Code也不是没有挑战。Claude Code已经积累了大量企业用户和开发者口碑，Anthropic在代码理解和长上下文方面的能力有目共睹；OpenAI Codex有GPT-5.6系列模型加持，编程能力是第一梯队；Cursor等创业公司已经在产品体验上打磨了很久，用户粘性很高。Meta作为后来者，能不能靠价格和架构优势快速突围，还要打个问号。

但对于开发者和企业来说，竞争越激烈越好。垄断只会带来高价和低质，充分竞争才能让产品越来越好、价格越来越低。AI编程工具的价格战，可能马上就要开始了。

明天见。
briefs.body_html_en:
Another heavyweight has entered the AI coding agent arena.

On August 5, Meta officially launched its first AI coding agent product, Muse Code, opening public beta. This is the first major product delivery since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang joined Meta earlier this year to lead its superintelligence lab. The goal is crystal clear: be a cheaper alternative to Claude Code and OpenAI Codex.

Zuckerberg was direct in his social media announcement: "Muse Code helps you complete real software engineering tasks across large codebases, not just autocomplete a few lines." From what's been released so far, this isn't another Copilot-style autocomplete tool — it's a full-fledged agent that can autonomously handle refactoring, debugging, and new feature development end-to-end.

Persistent Background Agents: What's the Core Differentiator?

Muse Code's biggest technical highlight is its persistent background agents architecture.

What does that mean? Most AI coding tools on the market today (including Claude Code and early Codex) work like this: you send a command, it spawns a new agent instance, completes the task, and then that instance is destroyed. Next time you send a command, it's a brand new agent with no memory of what you did last time, what your codebase looks like, or what your coding style is.

Muse Code is different. Its agents run persistently in the background — they continuously learn your codebase structure, remember your previous modification preferences, understand your project's architectural design, and can even proactively spot issues in your code and suggest optimizations. Maintaining context across sessions is a critical architectural difference.

An analogy: other tools are like hiring a contract programmer every time you need work done; they finish and leave, and next time it's a different person. Muse Code is like hiring a full-time senior engineer who stays on your team and understands your project better the longer they work on it. For large codebases (million-line scale), this continuous context accumulation delivers massive efficiency gains — the agent doesn't need to spend huge numbers of tokens reindexing and understanding the codebase every single time.

The second differentiator is price. Meta hasn't announced specific pricing, but it explicitly says it will be "significantly lower" than Claude Code and Codex. Given Meta's consistent open-source and low-price strategy (the Llama model family is effectively the standard in open source), Muse Code will likely use price competition to grab market share quickly. For enterprise users, AI coding tool costs are already a significant line item — Uber burning through its entire annual AI coding budget in four months is still fresh in everyone's memory. A cheaper alternative is enormously attractive.

AI Coding Moves from the Copilot Era to the Agent Era

Muse Code's entry marks AI coding's official transition from the "Copilot era" to the "Agent era."

2021–2024 was the Copilot era: AI's role was "assistant." You write code, it autocomplete; you need to watch, correct, and guide it constantly. Humans were fundamentally in charge, and AI was an accelerator. Starting in late 2025, we entered the Agent era: AI's role became "executor." You give a high-level task description, and it breaks it down, plans, writes code, runs tests, debugs on its own, and you just review the result.

Claude Code was the first benchmark product of this era; it proved AI agents could genuinely complete complex software engineering tasks in real production environments. OpenAI Codex followed close behind, leveraging the GPT model family to catch up quickly. Now Muse Code charges in, joining Cursor, Windsurf, Aider, and a host of startup products — the AI coding agent track is already crowded.

But Meta has advantages no one else can match. First, it has the Llama open-source model ecosystem — Muse Code can run on Llama 4 under the hood, and enterprise customers can deploy privately without worrying about leaking code to third parties. Second, Alexandr Wang's arrival brings Scale AI's deep expertise in data annotation and model evaluation — the most critical capability for an AI coding agent isn't writing code, it's knowing whether the code it wrote is correct, and Scale's evaluation capabilities directly fill that gap. Third, Meta itself is one of the world's largest code producers — Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp are all-hundred-million-user products, and Muse Code can be refined internally across billions of lines of code before being opened externally. That's an advantage pure startups don't have.

"In 2024 everyone competed on whose autocomplete was more accurate; in 2026 everyone competes on whose agent can independently ship a complete feature."— An AI coding tool founder

Of course, Muse Code isn't without challenges. Claude Code has already built up substantial enterprise users and developer reputation; Anthropic's capabilities in code understanding and long context are well-documented. OpenAI Codex has the GPT-5.6 model family backing it, with first-tier coding ability. Startups like Cursor have been polishing product experience for a long time and have high user stickiness. As a latecomer, whether Meta can break through quickly on price and architecture remains an open question.

But for developers and enterprises, more competition is always better. Monopoly only brings high prices and low quality; genuine competition makes products better and cheaper. The price war in AI coding tools may be about to begin.

See you tomorrow.

briefs.body_html:
视频生成领域的"DeepSeek时刻"，可能真的来了。

8月5日，清华系AI创业公司Sand.ai发布并完全开源了千亿级视频生成模型MAGI-2 Preview。创始人曹越是Swin Transformer的共同一作，在计算机视觉领域是成名已久的大佬。这次他们放出的东西，参数规模和效果都接近闭源第一梯队，但生成成本直接打到了主流模型的十分之一。

具体数字很夸张：总参数1140亿（114B），单次前向激活约60亿参数；生成一段10秒1080P视频的成本约0.5元人民币——而现在市面上主流闭源视频模型（Sora、Kling、Runway Gen-3）生成同样规格视频的成本大约是5-8元。十分之一的价格，效果还接近第一梯队，AA视频生成榜单排名第六。李开复看完直接给出评价："这就是AI视频生成界的DeepSeek。"

为什么视频模型不能照抄LLM的Scaling路线？

MAGI-2最核心的突破不是参数大，而是它证明了：视频生成的Scaling不能照抄LLM的路线，必须从底层重构架构。

过去一年多，很多公司做视频生成模型都是在LLM的架构上修修补补——把文本token换成视频token，把大语言模型的Transformer直接拿来做视频生成。结果是什么？模型越做越大，训练和推理成本飙升，但生成效果的提升却边际递减。更长的视频、更高的分辨率、更好的时序一致性，每一项都要付出指数级增长的算力代价。这就是视频生成的"不可能三角"：更大的模型、更长的视频、可控的成本，三者你最多选两个。

MAGI-2用MoE（Mixture of Experts，混合专家）架构打破了这个三角。但不是简单把LLM里的MoE搬过来——他们设计了专门针对视频的Multi-Head LatentMoE架构，还有三个关键创新：

第一，单流统一Transformer。文本、视频、音频三种模态用同一个主干网络处理，不是三个独立的编码器拼接。这意味着模型能更原生地理解文本描述和视频内容、音频之间的对应关系，多模态对齐效果更好。

第二，自研MagiMoE kernel库。MoE架构的推理效率一直是个大问题——路由选择、专家并行、负载均衡任何一个环节做不好，都会导致MoE比稠密模型还慢。Sand.ai没有用现成的MoE实现，而是从头写了专门针对视频生成场景优化的kernel，把激活稀疏性的效率吃到了极致。

第三，视频时序建模的特殊优化。视频和文本最大的区别是有时序维度——帧与帧之间必须连贯，不能闪烁、不能跳变、不能物体突然消失又出现。MAGI-2在注意力机制里加入了专门的时序一致性约束，不需要靠大量后处理就能生成比较稳定的长视频。

这三个创新加在一起，才实现了"千亿参数但推理成本极低"的效果。114B总参数听起来吓人，但每次生成只激活6B左右的参数，相当于用6B模型的成本跑出了接近千亿模型的效果。这就是MoE架构的威力，也是为什么DeepSeek、Mistral等公司在LLM领域早就用MoE把成本打下来了，而视频领域直到现在才有人真正做对。

开源视频模型的冲击波

MAGI-2完全开源（模型权重在GitHub和HuggingFace都可以下载），这件事的影响可能比模型本身的效果还大。

"当一个效果接近第一梯队的视频模型可以免费下载、在消费级GPU上跑起来的时候，所有闭源视频公司的定价模型都要重写。"—— 一位AI视频领域投资人

第一波冲击是价格。现在Sora、Kling、Runway的定价还是"按秒收费"的奢侈品逻辑，生成一分钟高质量视频要几百块钱。MAGI-2把成本打到十分之一，而且开源意味着任何人都可以基于它做二次开发、部署自己的视频生成服务——未来一年，视频生成API的价格大概率会像当年的大模型API一样雪崩式下跌。视频生成从"专业人士的工具"变成"人人用得起的基础设施"，这一步可能比所有人预想的都快。

第二波冲击是生态。开源模型会催生出大量的垂直应用：短视频创作者用它批量生成素材、电商平台用它批量做商品视频、广告公司用它快速出片、教育公司用它做课程视频。就像Stable Diffusion开源后图片生成领域爆发了几百个创业公司一样，视频生成领域的创业浪潮，可能马上就要被MAGI-2点爆。

当然，MAGI-2现在还是Preview版本，AA榜单排第六，和Sora、Kling这些闭源第一梯队比还有差距——特别是复杂运动场景、长视频一致性、文本渲染这些老大难问题，它还没有完全解决。但它证明了一件事：视频生成不需要闭源、不需要天价算力、不需要垄断，用创新的架构设计和开源的方式，同样能做出接近顶级水平的东西。

这就是开源的力量。当年Llama开源彻底改变了大模型的竞争格局，MAGI-2会不会对视频生成领域做同样的事？我们拭目以待。

明天见。
briefs.body_html_en:
The "DeepSeek moment" for video generation may have genuinely arrived.

On August 5, Tsinghua-backed AI startup Sand.ai released and fully open-sourced the hundred-billion-parameter video generation model MAGI-2 Preview. Founder Cao Yue is a co-first author of Swin Transformer and a long-established figure in computer vision. What they've delivered this time approaches closed-source first-tier quality in parameter scale and output, while driving generation costs down to one-tenth of mainstream models.

The numbers are striking: 114 billion (114B) total parameters, with roughly 6 billion parameters activated per forward pass; generating a 10-second 1080P video costs about 0.5 RMB (~$0.07) — while current mainstream closed-source video models (Sora, Kling, Runway Gen-3) charge roughly 5–8 RMB for the same specification. One-tenth the price, near first-tier quality, ranked sixth on the AA video generation leaderboard. Kai-Fu Lee saw it and immediately offered his assessment: "This is the DeepSeek of AI video generation."

Why Video Models Can't Just Copy LLM Scaling

MAGI-2's core breakthrough isn't parameter scale; it's proving that video generation scaling can't simply copy the LLM playbook — architecture has to be rebuilt from the ground up.

Over the past year-plus, many companies building video generation models have been tinkering with LLM architectures — replacing text tokens with video tokens and taking large language model Transformers directly to video generation. The result? Models got bigger, training and inference costs skyrocketed, but improvements in generation quality hit diminishing returns. Longer videos, higher resolutions, better temporal consistency — every increment required exponentially more compute. This is video generation's "impossible triangle": bigger models, longer videos, controllable costs — pick any two.

MAGI-2 breaks this triangle with MoE (Mixture of Experts) architecture. But it didn't simply port MoE from LLMs — they designed a Multi-Head LatentMoE purpose-built for video, with three key innovations:

First, unified single-stream Transformer. Text, video, and audio are processed by the same backbone network rather than three separate encoders stitched together. This means the model natively understands correspondences between text descriptions, video content, and audio, yielding better multimodal alignment.

Second, a custom MagiMoE kernel library. MoE inference efficiency has long been a problem — routing, expert parallelism, load balancing; any weak link makes MoE slower than dense models. Sand.ai didn't use off-the-shelf MoE implementations; they wrote kernels from scratch optimized specifically for video generation scenarios, pushing activation sparsity efficiency to its limits.

Third, specialized optimization for video temporal modeling. The biggest difference between video and text is the temporal dimension — frames must be coherent; no flickering, no jumping, no objects disappearing and reappearing. MAGI-2 adds specific temporal consistency constraints in the attention mechanism, generating relatively stable long videos without heavy post-processing.

These three innovations together deliver the "hundred-billion parameters, ultra-low inference cost" effect. 114B total parameters sounds intimidating, but only around 6B parameters activate per generation — meaning you get near-hundred-billion model quality at 6B-model cost. That's the power of MoE architecture, and it's why DeepSeek, Mistral, and others already drove costs down dramatically in LLMs, while in video, nobody truly got it right until now.

The Shockwave of an Open-Source Video Model

MAGI-2 being fully open source (model weights downloadable on both GitHub and HuggingFace) may have a bigger impact than the model's quality itself.

"When a video model approaching first-tier quality can be downloaded for free and run on consumer GPUs, every closed-source video company's pricing model gets rewritten."— An AI video investor

The first shockwave is pricing. Sora, Kling, and Runway are still priced on a luxury "per-second" logic — generating a minute of high-quality video costs hundreds of yuan. MAGI-2 drives costs to one-tenth, and open source means anyone can build on it, deploy their own video generation services. Over the next year, video generation API prices will likely collapse the same way LLM API prices did. Video generation going from "professional tool" to "infrastructure everyone can afford" may happen faster than anyone expected.

The second shockwave is ecosystem. Open-source models will spawn massive vertical applications: short-video creators using it to batch-generate footage, e-commerce platforms using it to produce product videos at scale, ad agencies using it for quick turnarounds, education companies using it for course videos. Just as Stable Diffusion's open-sourcing spawned hundreds of startups in image generation, the startup wave in video generation may be about to detonate, ignited by MAGI-2.

Of course, MAGI-2 is still a Preview release, ranked sixth on the AA leaderboard — it still lags behind closed-source first-tier models like Sora and Kling, particularly on hard problems like complex motion scenes, long-video consistency, and text rendering. But it proves one thing: video generation doesn't require closed source, doesn't require sky-high compute budgets, doesn't require monopoly; innovative architecture design and open source can still produce near-top-tier results.

That's the power of open source. Llama going open source fundamentally changed the competitive landscape for foundation models. Will MAGI-2 do the same for video generation? We'll find out soon.

See you tomorrow.

briefs.body_html:
自研AI芯片，正在从前卫选择变成前沿AI公司的标配。

8月5日，Anthropic官方确认正在组建内部定制芯片团队，为Claude系列模型设计专用AI芯片。芯片设计岗位的招聘信息已经挂出，年薪范围32万到48.5万美元——这个价格在芯片行业也算顶级待遇了，和NVIDIA、Apple的资深工程师薪酬持平。

此前The Information曾报道Anthropic与三星接触，洽谈潜在的芯片制造合作。TechCrunch的报道确认了这一消息，并表示Anthropic的目标不是做通用GPU，而是针对Claude的推理和训练 workload 做软硬件协同设计（co-design），让模型运行得更快、更省电、成本更低。

从买GPU到造芯片：AI公司的产业链上移

Anthropic不是第一家自研芯片的AI公司，但它的入场标志着一个趋势的彻底确立：前沿AI公司正在系统性地向上游突围，从"买GPU的客户"变成"设计芯片的玩家"。

我们来梳理一下时间线：Google从2015年开始就用自研的TPU，是这条路的先行者；Meta有MTIA加速器，已经迭代了几代；亚马逊AWS有Trainium和Inferentia；微软在研发Maia芯片；OpenAI在今年6月发布了和Broadcom合作设计的Jalapeño推理芯片；现在Anthropic也加入了战局。

为什么所有公司都开始自研芯片？三个根本原因。

第一，通用GPU的效率天花板。NVIDIA的GPU是为图形渲染和通用并行计算设计的，不是专门为大模型的推理和训练优化的。大模型的计算模式其实非常有规律——大部分时间在做矩阵乘法，注意力机制有固定的内存访问模式，KV缓存有特定的优化空间。一个专门为Transformer架构设计的ASIC芯片，在特定workload上可以做到GPU的3-5倍性能、1/3到1/5的功耗。Google TPU已经证明了这一点，OpenAI的Jalapeño据说推理效率是同功耗H100的4倍以上。

第二，供应链安全和成本控制。NVIDIA的GPU不仅贵（H100一颗3-4万美元，B200更贵），而且供不应求——产能被台积电CoWoS封装卡着，订单排到一年以后。如果你的业务完全依赖NVIDIA一家供应商，不仅成本下不来，供应链安全也是个大问题。万一哪天NVIDIA产能优先供给别的客户、或者对中国等特定地区断供、或者出了什么bug要召回，你的整个业务就停摆了。自研芯片虽然前期投入大（几亿到几十亿美元级别），但长期来看能大幅降低算力成本，还能保证供应链自主可控。

第三，软硬件协同的护城河。当你自己设计芯片、自己训练模型、自己做框架优化的时候，你可以做到通用GPU永远做不到的深度协同优化。比如你可以在芯片指令集层面直接支持Transformer里的FlashAttention、可以在硬件层面做KV缓存压缩、可以针对自己模型的稀疏性模式做专门优化。这种软硬件深度绑定带来的性能优势，是买通用GPU永远追不上的——苹果的M系列芯片在消费电子领域已经证明了这一点。

"2023年比谁融到的钱多，2024年比谁拿到的GPU多，2026年比谁自己能造芯片。AI军备竞赛的门槛，一年比一年高。"—— 一位半导体行业分析师

Anthropic的优势与挑战

Anthropic现在入场造芯，有自己的优势，也有巨大的挑战。

优势在于：第一，它不需要从零开始——已经和Broadcom等芯片设计服务公司有合作（OpenAI的Jalapeño也是Broadcom设计的），可以利用成熟的设计团队和IP，不需要自己养几千人的芯片设计团队；第二，它已经和AWS、Google、NVIDIA、AMD都签了大规模算力采购协议，自研芯片是补充不是替代，没有"all in自研"的生存压力，可以从容迭代；第三，Claude系列模型的架构是公开透明的（Anthropic发表了大量论文），团队对自己模型的计算特征了如指掌，软硬件协同优化的方向很清晰。

挑战也很明显。第一，芯片设计周期极长——从架构设计到流片到量产，通常需要2-3年。现在开始设计，真正用上可能要到2028-2029年，到时候模型架构会不会又变了？比如如果2-3年后主流模型从Transformer变成别的架构，今天设计的芯片可能就过时了。第二，人才竞争极其激烈——现在AI芯片设计师是全球最稀缺的人才，NVIDIA、Apple、AMD、Qualcomm、OpenAI、Google都在抢人，年薪48.5万美元能不能招到足够多的顶级人才，要打个问号。第三，制造端依赖台积电——三星的4nm/3nm工艺良率和台积电还有差距，如果找三星代工，芯片性能可能不如台积电的竞品。

但这些挑战挡不住趋势。AI发展到今天，算力已经不是"成本中心"而是"核心竞争力"了。一家前沿AI公司如果不能在算力层面有自己的独门秘籍，未来的竞争会越来越被动。Anthropic在和Volta签完100亿美元算力长约、和SpaceX、TeraWulf锁定电力之后，又开始自研芯片——这是一套完整的全栈算力布局。

AI军备竞赛，已经从算法层烧到了芯片层。

明天见。
briefs.body_html_en:
Custom AI silicon is going from avant-garde choice to standard equipment for frontier AI companies.

On August 5, Anthropic officially confirmed it's building an internal custom chip team to design purpose-built AI silicon for the Claude model family. Job listings for chip design roles are already posted, with annual compensation ranging from $320,000 to $485,000 — top-tier pay in the semiconductor industry, on par with senior engineer compensation at NVIDIA and Apple.

The Information previously reported Anthropic was in talks with Samsung about potential chip manufacturing partnership. TechCrunch's reporting confirmed this, stating that Anthropic's goal isn't to build general-purpose GPUs but to pursue hardware-software co-design specifically for Claude's inference and training workloads, making models run faster, more power-efficient, and cheaper.

From Buying GPUs to Building Chips: AI Companies Move Upstream

Anthropic isn't the first AI company to build custom chips, but its entry marks a trend firmly established: frontier AI companies are systematically pushing upstream, transforming from "GPU buyers" into "chip designers."

Let's walk through the timeline: Google has used custom TPUs since 2015, pioneering this path; Meta has the MTIA accelerator, iterated across several generations; Amazon AWS has Trainium and Inferentia; Microsoft is developing the Maia chip; OpenAI launched the Broadcom-partnered Jalapeño inference chip in June; and now Anthropic joins the fray.

Why is every company building custom chips? Three fundamental reasons.

First, the efficiency ceiling of general-purpose GPUs. NVIDIA GPUs were designed for graphics rendering and general-purpose parallel computing, not specifically optimized for LLM inference and training. LLM computation patterns are actually quite regular — most time is spent on matrix multiplication, attention has fixed memory access patterns, KV caching has specific optimization opportunities. An ASIC purpose-built for Transformer architectures can deliver 3–5x performance at 1/3 to 1/5 power consumption on specific workloads. Google's TPUs already proved this; OpenAI's Jalapeño is rumored to deliver over 4x inference efficiency per watt versus H100.

Second, supply chain security and cost control. NVIDIA GPUs aren't just expensive (H100s run $30–40K each; B200s cost more) — they're also supply-constrained, with production bottlenecked by TSMC CoWoS packaging and order backlogs stretching over a year. If your entire business depends on a single supplier (NVIDIA), not only can't you bring costs down, supply chain security becomes a critical issue. If NVIDIA prioritizes other customers, cuts off supply to certain regions, or has a recall, your entire operation grinds to a halt. Building custom chips requires massive upfront investment (hundreds of millions to billions), but long-term it dramatically reduces compute costs and ensures supply chain autonomy.

Third, the moat of hardware-software co-design. When you design your own chips, train your own models, and build your own framework optimizations, you can achieve deep co-optimization that general-purpose GPUs can never match. For example, you can directly support FlashAttention at the chip instruction set level, implement KV cache compression in hardware, or specialize for your model's sparsity patterns. This kind of deep hardware-software binding creates performance advantages that buying general-purpose GPUs can never catch up to — Apple's M-series chips already proved this in consumer electronics.

"2023 was about who raised more money; 2024 was about who got more GPUs; 2026 is about who can build their own chips. The barriers to entry in the AI arms race get higher every year."— A semiconductor industry analyst

Anthropic's Advantages and Challenges

Entering the chip race now, Anthropic has its advantages and also significant challenges.

On the advantage side: First, it doesn't have to start from zero — it can partner with design services firms like Broadcom (OpenAI's Jalapeño was also designed with Broadcom), leveraging mature design teams and IP without maintaining a multi-thousand-person chip design organization in-house. Second, it already has large-scale compute agreements with AWS, Google, NVIDIA, and AMD; custom silicon is a supplement, not a replacement, so there's no existential "all-in on custom chips" pressure, and it can iterate deliberately. Third, the Claude model family's architecture is transparent and well-published (Anthropic has released extensive technical papers); the team intimately understands its models' computational characteristics, giving clear direction for hardware-software co-optimization.

The challenges are also obvious. First, chip design cycles are extremely long — from architecture to tapeout to mass production typically takes 2–3 years. Starting now, real deployment might not happen until 2028–2029. Will model architectures have changed again by then? If the dominant architecture shifts away from Transformers in 2–3 years, chips designed today could be obsolete. Second, talent competition is ferocious — AI chip designers are the scarcest talent on the planet; NVIDIA, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, OpenAI, and Google are all competing. Whether $485K can attract enough top talent remains an open question. Third, manufacturing depends on TSMC — Samsung's 4nm/3nm yields still lag behind TSMC, and manufacturing with Samsung could mean performance gaps versus TSMC-built competitors.

But none of these challenges will stop the trend. AI has reached a point where compute is no longer a "cost center" but a "core competency." A frontier AI company that doesn't have its own secret sauce at the compute level will be increasingly disadvantaged. After signing a $10B long-term compute deal with Volta and locking in power with SpaceX and TeraWulf, Anthropic is now designing custom chips — this is a complete full-stack compute strategy.

The AI arms race has burned from the algorithm layer up to the silicon layer.

See you tomorrow.

briefs.body_html:
8月4日盘后，马斯克交出了SpaceX上市后的第一份季度成绩单。数字很炸裂，市场反应却很微妙。

先看好消息：Q2总营收78.14亿美元，同比增长92%，大幅超出市场预期的69亿美元；调整后EBITDA首次转正（Q1还是-6亿美元）；AI业务收入25.61亿美元，同比暴增247%，占总营收约三分之一。Starlink用户数突破700万，发射业务继续保持全球第一。

再看坏消息：季度AI资本开支约158亿美元，平均每天在AI上砸1.7亿美元。马斯克明确表示SpaceX"只用英伟达GPU"，Colossus数据中心还在疯狂扩建。财报发布后，SpaceX盘后股价下跌7-8%——营收超预期，但市场被百亿美元级别的烧钱速度吓坏了。

卖GPU算力，比发射火箭更赚钱？

这份财报最有意思的地方不是火箭发射，而是SpaceX的身份正在发生根本性转变：它正在从一家"火箭公司"变成一家"AI算力公司"。

AI业务25.6亿美元的季度收入是怎么来的？答案是Colossus数据中心的算力转售。SpaceX在得克萨斯州建设的Colossus超算集群，目前已经是全球最大的GPU集群之一（超过10万块H100/B200），主要客户是Anthropic、xAI以及其他需要大规模算力的AI公司。简单来说：SpaceX买英伟达的GPU，建数据中心，然后把GPU小时卖给AI公司——本质上是个"算力批发商"。

这个生意有多赚钱？看毛利率就知道了。火箭发射业务的毛利率大约在20-30%（因为火箭制造成本、燃料、发射场运营都很贵），Starlink的毛利率在40-50%左右（卫星折旧是主要成本），而算力转售业务的毛利率据说能达到60-70%——一旦数据中心建起来，后续的主要成本就是电费和运维，边际成本很低。难怪马斯克要在AI上砸这么多钱，这确实是比发射火箭更好的生意。

马斯克自己也承认："我们没想到卖GPU算力会这么赚钱。"Colossus一期刚上线就被Anthropic等客户包圆了，二期、三期还在建设中，预订已经排到了2028年。AI算力现在是卖方市场，只要你有电、有GPU、能快速交付，客户排队给你送钱。

1.7亿美元一天：市场在怕什么？

既然AI算力这么赚钱，为什么财报发布后股价反而跌了？因为市场看到了一个让人脊背发凉的数字：158亿美元的季度AI资本开支。

"当一家公司每天在GPU上花1.7亿美元，你第一个想到的问题不是'它能赚多少钱'，而是'这个泡沫什么时候破'。"—— 一位华尔街科技分析师

158亿美元是什么概念？这比很多Fortune 500强公司一整年的营收还高。这是单季度的资本开支，不是年度的。按这个烧钱速度，SpaceX一年在AI上的投入超过600亿美元——相当于OpenAI全年营收的好几倍。

市场的担忧主要有三个。

第一，投入产出比的不确定性。现在AI算力确实供不应求，但这个供需失衡能持续多久？如果未来2-3年大量数据中心建成、GPU产能上来、或者算法效率大幅提升（比如小模型效果追平大模型），算力价格可能会像云服务价格一样持续下跌。今天砸几百亿美元建的数据中心，3年后会不会变成昂贵的废铁？

第二，客户集中度风险。SpaceX的算力收入高度依赖少数几个大客户（Anthropic是最大客户，据传xAI也在用）。如果Anthropic未来转用其他供应商、或者自己建数据中心、或者融资烧完了，SpaceX的算力收入可能会断崖式下跌。单一客户占比过高，这是所有B2B基础设施生意的大忌。

第三，马斯克的管理精力分散。马斯克现在同时管着Tesla、SpaceX、xAI、Neuralink、The Boring Company、Twitter/X六家公司，其中SpaceX和xAI都在疯狂烧钱建数据中心。一个人的精力是有限的，同时管这么多百亿美元级别的超级项目，会不会出问题？历史上很少有企业家能同时管好两家千亿美元公司，更别说六家。

但马斯克显然不这么想。他在财报电话会上的表态非常激进："AI算力是21世纪的石油，现在的投入不是太多，而是太少。我们会继续加速建设Colossus，未来四个季度的AI资本开支可能还会增加。"

这就是典型的马斯克式豪赌：要么all in赢者通吃，要么赌输了一起完蛋。华尔街喜欢这种故事，但也害怕这种故事。2000年互联网泡沫的时候，电信公司也是这样疯狂砸钱建光缆、建数据中心，结果泡沫一破，90%的产能闲置，股价跌去90%以上。AI算力会不会重蹈覆辙？现在没人知道。

但有一点是确定的：SpaceX已经不是你认识的那个只造火箭的公司了。它现在是AI算力军备竞赛里最激进的玩家之一。

明天见。
briefs.body_html_en:
After hours on August 4, Elon Musk delivered SpaceX's first quarterly report card since going public. The numbers are explosive, but the market reaction was nuanced.

First the good news: Q2 total revenue hit $7.814 billion, up 92% year-over-year, significantly beating consensus estimates of ~$6.9 billion; adjusted EBITDA turned positive for the first time (Q1 was -$600 million); AI business revenue reached $2.561 billion, surging 247% YoY and accounting for roughly one-third of total revenue. Starlink subscribers passed 7 million; launch business remains global number one.

Now the bad news: quarterly AI capital expenditure was approximately $15.8 billion, averaging $170 million per day spent on AI. Musk explicitly stated SpaceX uses "only NVIDIA GPUs," and the Colossus data center is still expanding furiously. After the earnings release, SpaceX stock dropped 7–8% after hours — revenue beat, but the market was terrified by the pace of spending in the tens of billions.

Selling GPU Compute Is More Profitable Than Launching Rockets?

The most interesting thing about this earnings report isn't rocket launches; it's that SpaceX's identity is fundamentally shifting: it's going from a "rocket company" to an "AI compute company."

Where does $2.56 billion in quarterly AI revenue come from? The answer is compute resale from the Colossus data center. SpaceX's Colossus supercomputing cluster in Texas is already one of the world's largest GPU clusters (over 100,000 H100/B200 GPUs), with primary customers being Anthropic, xAI, and other AI companies needing massive scale. Simply put: SpaceX buys NVIDIA GPUs, builds data centers, and resells GPU hours to AI companies — essentially a "compute wholesaler."

How profitable is this business? Gross margins tell the story. Rocket launch gross margins run around 20–30% (rocket manufacturing, fuel, launch pad operations are expensive); Starlink gross margins are around 40–50% (satellite depreciation is the main cost); compute resale gross margins are reportedly 60–70% — once the data center is built, ongoing costs are mainly electricity and operations with very low marginal cost. No wonder Musk is pouring this much money into AI; it really is a better business than launching rockets.

Musk himself admitted: "We didn't expect selling GPU compute would be this profitable." Colossus Phase 1 was fully booked by Anthropic and other customers immediately upon going live; Phases 2 and 3 are still under construction with reservations stretching to 2028. AI compute is currently a seller's market — if you have power, GPUs, and can deliver fast, customers are lined up throwing money at you.

$170 Million Per Day: What Is the Market Afraid Of?

If AI compute is this profitable, why did the stock drop after earnings? Because the market saw a spine-chilling number: $15.8 billion in quarterly AI capex.

"When a company is spending $170 million a day on GPUs, the first question you ask isn't 'how much money can it make,' it's 'when does this bubble pop.'"— A Wall Street tech analyst

What does $15.8 billion mean? It's more than the full-year revenue of many Fortune 500 companies. That's quarterly capex, not annual. At this burn rate, SpaceX is spending over $60 billion a year on AI — multiple times OpenAI's full-year revenue.

The market has three main concerns.

First, uncertainty around ROI. AI compute is indeed in short supply right now, but how long will this supply-demand imbalance last? If massive data center capacity comes online over the next 2–3 years, GPU production ramps up, or algorithm efficiency improves dramatically (e.g., small models catching up to large ones), compute prices could decline steadily the way cloud services prices have. Could the data centers being built for tens of billions today become expensive scrap metal three years from now?

Second, customer concentration risk. SpaceX's compute revenue depends heavily on a small number of large customers (Anthropic is the largest, with xAI reportedly also a major user). If Anthropic switches to other suppliers in the future, builds its own data centers, or burns through its funding, SpaceX's compute revenue could cliff-dive. Over-reliance on a single customer is a cardinal sin in any B2B infrastructure business.

Third, Musk's stretched management bandwidth. Musk is currently running Tesla, SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink, The Boring Company, and Twitter/X simultaneously — six companies, with SpaceX and xAI both burning cash building data centers at a ferocious pace. A person's bandwidth is finite; running this many multi-billion-dollar mega-projects simultaneously — how can it not go wrong? History shows few entrepreneurs can successfully run two $100B+ companies concurrently, let alone six.

But Musk clearly disagrees. His tone on the earnings call was aggressive: "AI compute is the oil of the 21st century. We're not spending too much — we're spending too little. We will continue accelerating Colossus construction; AI capex over the next four quarters may actually increase."

This is classic Musk-style all-in: bet everything for winner-take-all, or go down together. Wall Street loves this narrative but also fears it. During the dot-com bubble in 2000, telecom companies were similarly pouring money into fiber optic cables and data centers, and when the bubble popped, 90% of capacity went idle and stocks lost 90%+ of their value. Will AI compute repeat history? Nobody knows right now.

But one thing is certain: SpaceX is no longer the company you knew that only built rockets. It's now one of the most aggressive players in the AI compute arms race.

See you tomorrow.

briefs.body_html:
Tokenmaxxing这个词，可能要进历史书了。

2026年7月，微软执行副总裁Jay Parikh发出内部邮件，明确要求公司各业务部门设定"AI Token预算目标"，邮件里有一句话在硅谷疯传："Tokenmaxxing不是优化目标。"

什么是Tokenmaxxing？这个词是从互联网亚文化里的looksmaxxing（颜值最大化）、gymmaxxing（健身最大化）演变来的，意思是"Token使用量最大化"——鼓励员工尽可能多地消耗AI Token，用得越多说明你越拥抱AI、越先进。就在半年前，微软内部还有各种"AI使用排行榜"，Meta有"Claudeonomics"排行榜，OpenAI有员工一周处理2100亿token（相当于填满维基百科33遍）的"英雄事迹"被内部传颂。黄仁勋在多个场合公开倡导："年薪50万美元的工程师，每年应该消耗至少25万美元的token。"

现在，风向变了。

从"用得越多越好"到"算投入产出比"

微软不是第一个踩刹车的，但它是第一个明确喊停的大厂。

内部邮件显示，微软不仅给各部门设了Token预算上限，还把内部默认模型从之前的选项切换到了GPT-5.6——原因很简单：更便宜。员工现在可以在内部系统看到自己个人的AI token支出，很多工程师看到自己一个月花了几千美元在AI工具上，自己都吓了一跳。

Uber的例子更夸张。今年年初Uber给全年AI编程工具做了预算，结果到4月份就烧光了。Cursor等AI编程工具因为需求爆炸，报价涨了4-5倍。Uber后来不得不出台硬性规定：每人每种Agent工具每月限额1500美元，超了自己掏钱或者走特殊审批。Atlassian更夸张，月度AI支出不到一年增长了3倍，超过1500万美元。Adobe、Citi、Amazon等公司也都在悄悄收紧员工的AI使用权限。

为什么会突然转向？因为大家算完账发现一个尴尬的事实：Token消耗和生产率提升不是线性相关的。你给工程师无限量的AI额度，他可能会用AI写邮件、做PPT、写一些无关紧要的代码，甚至让AI帮他刷社交媒体文案——这些消耗了大量token，但并没有带来对应的产出。有工程师匿名承认：自己有30-40%的AI token花在了"和工作无关的事情上"。

"Tokenmaxxing时代大家比谁用AI用得多，ROI时代大家比谁用同样的token产出更多。这是企业AI从青春期进入成年期的标志。"—— 一位企业IT采购负责人

纳德拉今年6月在播客里承认自己也是个Tokenmaxxer——他承认自己每天用各种AI工具消耗大量token。但他话锋一转："问题不是你用了多少token，而是每花一美元在AI上，你赚回了多少美元。边际生产率收益必须匹配边际成本。"这句话从微软CEO嘴里说出来，基本上就是给Tokenmaxxing时代盖棺定论了。

企业AI落地的真实困境

微软带头设Token预算这件事，折射出企业AI落地过程中的一个普遍困境：大家都知道AI有用，但没人知道它到底值多少钱。

过去两年，企业采购AI工具基本上是"运动式"的——CEO喊一句"all in AI"，各部门就疯狂买licenses、上项目、搞培训，没人算ROI，因为算ROI就显得你"不拥抱变化""保守落后"。AI公司销售打单的时候最喜欢说的一句话就是："现在不布局AI，三年后你的公司就不存在了。"在这种焦虑营销下，企业的AI支出像脱缰的野马一样暴涨。

但到了2026年，上市公司要交财报了，CFO们开始算账了。一算发现不对：AI支出涨了5倍10倍，对应的生产率提升在哪里？成本节约在哪里？收入增长在哪里？很多时候答案是模糊的。员工确实在用AI，但到底是真的提升了效率，还是只是把原来的工作换了一种方式做？没人能说清楚。

这不是说AI没用。AI确实在编程、客服、内容创作、数据分析等场景带来了显著的效率提升。但问题是：提升了多少？值不值得这个价格？哪些场景ROI最高？哪些场景用AI纯属浪费钱？这些问题过去没人认真回答，现在CFO们要求答案了。

从刷token排行榜到设部门预算，从"用得越多越先进"到"每一分钱都要算ROI"，企业AI正在经历一次理性回归。这不是AI泡沫破了，而是AI落地进入了更健康的阶段——任何技术革命都要经历从hype到理性的过程，互联网是这样，云计算是这样，AI也不会例外。

黄仁勋说"工程师每年应该消耗25万美元token"，这句话在2025年是政治正确，在2026年你再说这句话，CFO会找你谈话。

明天见。
briefs.body_html_en:
The word "Tokenmaxxing" may be headed for the history books.

In July 2026, Microsoft executive vice president Jay Parikh sent an internal memo explicitly requiring business units to set "AI token budget targets." One line from the email went viral across Silicon Valley: "Tokenmaxxing is not an optimization goal."

What is Tokenmaxxing? The term evolved from internet subculture slang like looksmaxxing and gymmaxxing, meaning "maximizing token usage" — encouraging employees to consume as many AI tokens as possible; the more you used, the more you were embracing AI, the more advanced you were. Just half a year ago, Microsoft still had internal "AI usage leaderboards"; Meta had a "Claudeonomics" leaderboard; at OpenAI, an employee's "heroic" week processing 210 billion tokens (enough to fill Wikipedia 33 times over) was celebrated internally. Jensen Huang publicly advocated on multiple occasions: "An engineer making $500K a year should consume at least $250K in tokens annually."

Now the winds have shifted.

From "More Is Better" to "Counting ROI"

Microsoft wasn't the first to hit the brakes, but it was the first big tech company to explicitly call time.

Internal memos show Microsoft not only set token budget caps for departments but also switched the internal default model from previous options to GPT-5.6 — for a simple reason: it's cheaper. Employees can now see their personal AI token spending in internal systems; many engineers were shocked to discover they were spending thousands of dollars a month on AI tools.

Uber's example is even more dramatic. At the start of the year, Uber budgeted for full-year AI coding tools; by April, the budget was gone. Cursor and other AI coding tools raised prices 4–5x as demand exploded. Uber eventually had to impose hard rules: $1,500 per person per month per Agent tool; over that limit and you pay out of pocket or go through special approval. Atlassian is even more extreme — monthly AI spending tripled in less than a year to over $15 million. Adobe, Citi, and Amazon are also quietly tightening employee AI usage permissions.

Why the sudden pivot? Because when companies ran the numbers, they hit an awkward truth: token consumption and productivity gains are not linearly correlated. Give engineers unlimited AI access, and they might use AI to write emails, make PowerPoints, write trivial code, or even generate social media posts — consuming massive tokens without delivering corresponding output. Some engineers have admitted anonymously that 30–40% of their AI tokens are spent on "things unrelated to work."

"In the Tokenmaxxing era everyone competed on who used more AI; in the ROI era everyone competes on who gets more output from the same tokens. This is enterprise AI moving from adolescence to adulthood."— An enterprise IT procurement lead

Satya Nadella admitted on a podcast in June that he's a Tokenmaxxer himself — that he uses various AI tools daily consuming significant tokens. But then he pivoted: "The question isn't how many tokens you use; it's how many dollars you earn back for every dollar spent on AI. Marginal productivity gains must match marginal costs." Coming from Microsoft's CEO, this was essentially nailing the coffin shut on the Tokenmaxxing era.

The Real Challenges of Enterprise AI Adoption

Microsoft taking the lead on token budgets reflects a universal challenge in enterprise AI adoption: everyone knows AI is useful, but nobody knows exactly how much it's worth.

For the past two years, enterprise AI procurement was largely "campaign-style" — the CEO says "all in on AI," and departments go on a licensing, project, and training spree. Nobody calculated ROI because calculating ROI made you look like you "weren't embracing change" or were "conservative and backward." AI salespeople's favorite line was: "If you don't adopt AI now, your company won't exist in three years." Under this anxiety marketing, enterprise AI spending exploded like a runaway horse.

But in 2026, public companies have to report earnings, and CFOs started running the numbers. The math didn't add up: AI spending went up 5x or 10x, but where were the corresponding productivity gains? The cost savings? The revenue growth? Too often the answer was vague. Employees were indeed using AI, but were they genuinely more efficient, or just doing the same work differently? Nobody could say for sure.

This isn't to say AI is useless. AI has delivered significant efficiency gains in coding, customer service, content creation, data analysis, and other scenarios. But the question is: how much gain? Is it worth the price? Which scenarios have the highest ROI? Which scenarios are pure waste when using AI? These questions weren't seriously answered before, and now CFOs are demanding answers.

From token leaderboards to departmental budgets, from "more usage = more advanced" to "every penny must show ROI," enterprise AI is going through a rational correction. This isn't the AI bubble popping; it's AI adoption entering a healthier phase. Every technology revolution goes through hype to rationalization — the internet did it, cloud computing did it, and AI won't be an exception.

Jensen Huang saying "engineers should spend $250K a year on tokens" was politically correct in 2025. Say it in 2026, and the CFO will want a word.

See you tomorrow.

briefs.body_html:
A股终于等来了人形机器人第一股。

8月5日，宇树科技正式启动科创板IPO初步询价。网上网下申购时间为8月10日，发行估值约420亿元人民币，预计发行价约104元/股，一签缴款约5.2万元。8月7日举行网上路演，中信证券担任主承销商和保荐人，预计8月下旬正式挂牌上市。

这是A股第一家真正意义上专注于人形机器人领域的上市公司。在此之前，A股的"机器人概念股"要么是做工业机器人关节的零部件厂商，要么是蹭热点的传统制造企业，真正做通用人形机器人整机并且能量产的，宇树是第一家。

从春晚机器狗到人形机器人：王兴兴的硬核创业路

宇树科技的故事，是中国硬科技创业的一个典型样本。

创始人王兴兴是85后，上海大学硕士毕业，在机器人圈子里是成名已久的"技术狂人"。2016年他在深圳创办宇树科技，最早做四足机器人（机器狗），是全球最早把四足机器人做到消费级价位的公司之一。2021年春晚，宇树的机器牛"犇犇"登上春晚舞台和刘德华、王一博同台表演，一战成名——那是大众第一次意识到：中国的机器人技术已经做到这个水平了。

真正让宇树火出圈的是2023年以后的人形机器人赛道。宇树先后发布了H1、G1等多款人形机器人产品，售价从几万到几十万人民币不等，是全球价格最低的量产人形机器人之一。和特斯拉Optimus还在实验室阶段、波士顿动力的机器人贵到买不起不同，宇树的人形机器人已经卖到了全球几十个国家，被高校、研究机构、科技公司买去做二次开发和研究。

宇树最核心的竞争力是全产业链自研：电机、减速器、控制器、整机结构、运动算法，几乎所有核心零部件和软件都是自己做的。这不仅大幅降低了成本（这是宇树能把价格打下来的根本原因），也让它在供应链上不被卡脖子。英伟达也是宇树的合作伙伴，Jetson系列芯片被用在宇树的多款机器人产品上。

具身智能资本化的拐点

宇树科技IPO不是一个孤立事件，它是2026年具身智能赛道整体爆发的一个缩影。

过去半年，人形机器人和具身智能领域的融资新闻密集到让人麻木：蚂蚁集团领投灵波科技15亿元A轮融资、LimX Dynamics完成20亿元pre-IPO轮融资、智元机器人、傅利叶智能、星动纪元等公司也都在推进资本化进程。政策层面，七部委联合印发了《人形机器人创新发展指导意见》，列出了24项重点发展任务，把人形机器人上升到了国家战略产业的高度。

"2023年人形机器人还在做后空翻demo，2026年就要IPO敲钟了。这个行业的发展速度，比所有人预想的都快。"—— 一位机器人行业投资人

资本市场为什么突然这么看好人形机器人？三个核心逻辑。

第一，大模型给机器人装上了"大脑"。以前的机器人只能做预设好的动作，遇到没见过的场景就傻了。多模态大模型成熟之后，机器人可以理解自然语言指令、识别陌生场景、自主规划任务路径——通用机器人的可能性第一次真正打开了。

第二，制造成本正在快速下降。两年前一台人形机器人成本还在几十万美元，现在宇树已经把量产版打到了几万人民币级别。成本曲线和电动车早期非常像——一开始是百万级的玩具，然后降到几十万、几万，最后进入消费级市场。如果未来3-5年人形机器人能降到一部手机的价格，市场空间是万亿级别的。

第三，场景开始落地。工业制造、物流仓储、安防巡检、家庭服务，越来越多的场景开始试点人形机器人。虽然现在还远没到大规模普及的程度，但方向已经很清晰了。就像2015年前后的电动车——那时候续航短、充电慢、价格贵，但所有人都知道这是未来。

当然，现在的人形机器人还处在非常早期的阶段——走路还偶尔会摔、手的精细操作还很笨拙、真正能做的有用工作还很有限。宇树420亿的估值也不便宜，肯定包含了大量对未来的预期。但资本投的从来不是现在，而是未来。

宇树敲钟的那一刻，具身智能赛道的资本化大幕，就算正式拉开了。

明天见。
briefs.body_html_en:
The A-share market finally has its first humanoid robot stock.

On August 5, Unitree Robotics officially launched the preliminary bookbuilding phase for its STAR Market IPO. Online and offline subscription opens August 10, with an offering valuation of approximately 42 billion RMB (~$5.8 billion), expected offering price around 104 RMB per share, requiring roughly 52,000 RMB per lot. The online roadshow takes place August 7, with CITIC Securities as lead underwriter and sponsor; the stock is expected to officially list in late August.

This is the first genuine A-share listed company focused on humanoid robots. Before this, A-share "robot concept stocks" were either component manufacturers making industrial robot joints or traditional manufacturing companies riding the hype. Unitree is the first to actually build mass-produced general-purpose humanoid robots as a complete product.

From Spring Festival Robot Dogs to Humanoids: Wang Xingxing's Hardcore Startup Journey

Unitree's story is a classic example of Chinese hard-tech entrepreneurship.

Founder Wang Xingxing, born in the late 80s, holds a master's from Shanghai University and is a long-recognized "tech maniac" in robotics circles. He founded Unitree in Shenzhen in 2016, starting with quadruped robots (robot dogs), and was one of the first companies globally to bring quadruped robots to consumer price points. During the 2021 Spring Festival Gala, Unitree's robot ox "Ben Ben" performed on stage alongside Andy Lau and Wang Yibo, becoming a household name overnight — that was when the general public first realized: Chinese robotics technology had reached this level.

What really made Unitree a breakout name was the humanoid robot track after 2023. Unitree released multiple humanoid robot products including the H1 and G1, priced from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of RMB, making them some of the world's most affordable mass-produced humanoid robots. Unlike Tesla's Optimus, which is still in the lab phase, and Boston Dynamics' robots, which are prohibitively expensive, Unitree's humanoid robots have been sold to dozens of countries, purchased by universities, research institutions, and tech companies for secondary development and research.

Unitree's core competitive advantage is full-stack in-house R&D: motors, reducers, controllers, mechanical structure, locomotion algorithms — virtually all core components and software are built in-house. This not only dramatically reduces costs (the fundamental reason Unitree can drive prices down) but also insulates it from supply chain bottlenecks. NVIDIA is also a Unitree partner; Jetson series chips are used in multiple Unitree robot products.

The Inflection Point for Embodied AI Capitalization

Unitree Robotics' IPO isn't an isolated event — it's a microcosm of the embodied AI sector's overall explosion in 2026.

Over the past six months, humanoid robot and embodied AI funding news has been coming so fast it's numbing: Ant Group led Lingbot Technology's 1.5 billion RMB Series A; LimX Dynamics closed a 2 billion RMB pre-IPO round; Agibot, Fourier Intelligence, Galaxy Bot, and other companies are all advancing capitalization plans. On the policy side, seven ministries jointly issued the "Guiding Opinions on Humanoid Robot Innovation and Development," listing 24 key development tasks and elevating humanoid robots to the level of a national strategic industry.

"In 2023 humanoid robots were still doing backflip demos; in 2026 they're about to ring the IPO bell. This industry is moving faster than anyone expected."— A robotics industry investor

Why is capital suddenly so bullish on humanoid robots? Three core logics.

First, foundation models gave robots a "brain." Previously robots could only perform pre-programmed actions and would freeze when encountering unfamiliar scenes. With the maturation of multimodal foundation models, robots can understand natural language instructions, recognize novel environments, and autonomously plan task paths — the possibility of general-purpose robots has genuinely opened up for the first time.

Second, manufacturing costs are dropping rapidly. Two years ago a humanoid robot cost hundreds of thousands of dollars; today Unitree has driven mass-produced versions down to tens of thousands of RMB. The cost curve looks very similar to early electric vehicles — starting as million-yuan toys, then dropping to hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and eventually reaching the consumer market. If humanoid robots can reach smartphone prices in 3–5 years, the market size will be in the trillions.

Third, use cases are starting to land. Industrial manufacturing, logistics warehousing, security patrolling, home service — more and more scenarios are piloting humanoid robots. While we're still far from mass adoption, the direction is clear. Just like electric vehicles around 2015 — back then range was short, charging was slow, prices were high, but everyone knew it was the future.

Of course, humanoid robots today are still at a very early stage — they still occasionally fall while walking, fine hand manipulation is still clumsy, and the truly useful tasks they can perform remain limited. Unitree's 42 billion RMB valuation isn't cheap; it definitely includes massive future expectations. But capital never invests in the present — it invests in the future.

The moment Unitree rings the bell, the capitalization curtain for embodied AI officially rises.

See you tomorrow.

cao.body_html:
朋友们，今天AI圈的魔幻现实主义大戏，主角换成了普华永道。

事情是这样的：有人发现普华永道中东分支机构（PwC Middle East）在2024到2026年间发布的4份专业研究报告，打开一看全是AI幻觉——虚构的概念、错误的数据引用、编得有鼻子有眼的参考文献、点不开的虚假脚注、张冠李戴的观点归因。最离谱的是其中一份叫《转型治理》（Transformation Governance）的报告，用AI检测工具跑了一下：正文部分100%由AI生成，没有一个字是人类写的。连改都没改，直接把ChatGPT的输出导出成PDF，盖上普华永道的公章，就当"专业研究报告"发给客户了。

朋友们，这就相当于你去米其林三星餐厅吃饭，菜单写着"主厨秘制松露和牛"，结果后厨给你上了一包加热完的料理包，还在包装上贴了个假产地标签——法国进口松露，实际是河南产的香菇酱。

而且这不是实习生手滑发错了文件，这是4份报告，时间跨度两年，主题涉及人工智能、电动汽车这些前沿领域。也就是说，整整两年时间里，普华永道中东整个团队，从写报告的顾问到审核的经理到签字的合伙人，没有一个人发现——或者说，没有一个人在乎——这些报告是AI编的。

AI幻觉砸了专业服务的金字招牌

为什么这事特别讽刺？因为普华永道是谁？是全球四大会计师事务所之首，是"专业""严谨""可信"的代名词。上市公司的财报要他们审计才敢发，跨国并购要他们做尽职调查才敢签，企业花几百万几千万请他们做咨询，买的就是他们三个字：可信度。

现在你告诉我，他们盖着公章发出去的报告，连参考文献都是编的？

我们来看看这些报告里具体有什么离谱内容：有报告里提到一个"行业通用的AI治理框架"，框架名字听起来很高大上，结果搜遍全网根本不存在这个框架，是AI编的；有报告引用了一篇"2025年麦肯锡全球AI调研报告"，麦肯锡确实发过类似的报告，但报告里引用的数据和原文完全对不上，是AI自己瞎编的数字；还有的报告里列了十几篇参考文献，点链接进去要么是404，要么是和主题完全无关的论文，甚至连作者名字都是编的。

最搞笑的是AI编的一个"专家观点"，说"哈佛商学院Smith教授在2025年的研究表明……"，结果有人去查了哈佛商学院近五年的教授名单，根本没有一个叫Smith的教授做过相关研究。AI不仅编了研究结论，连人都给你编出来了。

"以前我们担心AI会取代专业人士，现在看来AI先取代了专业人士的工作态度。"—— 一位管理咨询顾问

这事给所有用AI的人提了三个醒

普华永道翻车不是孤例，它是AI普及过程中必然会出现的乱象。只不过这次翻车的是最不该翻车的专业机构，所以格外有警示意义。给所有用AI写东西的朋友提三个醒：

第一，专业内容领域，AI生成必须100%人工审核。AI是很好的写作助手，可以帮你列大纲、找思路、写初稿，但任何要对外发布的专业内容——报告、白皮书、研报、客户交付物——必须经过有专业能力的人类逐字审核。AI会非常自信地编造事实、引用不存在的文献、给出错误的数据，这不是bug，这是现在大模型的本质特性。普华永道这次的问题不是"用了AI"，而是"用了AI之后连看都没看就发出去了"。

第二，不要盲目信任大牌机构的产出。很多人看到"普华永道""麦肯锡""波士顿咨询"的logo就觉得内容一定靠谱，现在这个时代不对了。大牌机构也是人在干活，人会偷懒，会有侥幸心理，会为了赶deadline走捷径。以后看到任何机构的报告，尤其是涉及AI、新能源这些快速变化领域的报告，多长个心眼——关键数据点自己去交叉验证一下，参考文献点进去看看是不是真的存在。

第三，AI时代，"认真"这两个字反而更值钱了。当所有人都在用AI一键生成内容的时候，那些愿意花时间核实事实、核对数据、打磨观点、对自己产出的每一个字负责的人，反而会变得更加稀缺和珍贵。AI降低了内容生产的门槛，但没有降低"好内容"的门槛。真正的专业主义不是看你用什么工具写的，而是看你对你写的东西有没有敬畏心。

据说普华永道中东已经开始内部调查了，相关团队的负责人可能会被问责。但这个事情造成的信誉损失，不是开除几个人就能补回来的。毕竟客户请你做专业服务，买的是你的判断力和责任心，不是你按"生成"按钮的速度。

今天就槽到这里，明天继续。
